Hopkins test of clustering tendency for landmark shapes

Source: R/hopkins.R
hopkins_shape.Rd

Hopkins statistic with a Monte Carlo reference distribution, for a sample of shapes given as a real \(k \times d \times n\) landmark array (\(d = 2\) or \(3\)).

Usage

hopkins_shape(
  X,
  null = c("tangent", "uniform"),
  m = NULL,
  power = NULL,
  B = 199,
  distance = "rho",
  seed = NULL
)

Arguments

X

Numeric array \(k \times d \times n\), \(d \in \{2, 3\}\).

null

"tangent" (default) or "uniform"; see Details.

m

Number of artificial and of sampled points. Default round(0.1 * n), at least 1.

power

Exponent \(p\); default 1.

B

Number of Monte Carlo reference draws.

distance

Shape distance ("rho", "dF", "dP") for null = "uniform". The tangent null uses Euclidean distance in the aligned coordinates.

seed

Optional integer seed; the caller's random-number stream is restored on exit.

Value

An object of class "hopkins_shape": a list with statistic, p.value, null, power, m, B, and reference (the B reference values).

Details

The statistic is \(H = \sum u^p / (\sum u^p + \sum w^p)\), where \(u\) are the nearest-neighbor distances from \(m\) artificial points to the data and \(w\) those from \(m\) sampled data points to the other data. Large values indicate clustering.

With null = "tangent", the artificial points come from a unimodal Gaussian with the mean and covariance of the Procrustes-aligned data coordinates (centered, unit-size configurations rotated onto the Procrustes mean), and distances are Euclidean in those coordinates. This tests unimodality against clustering. With null = "uniform", the artificial points are uniform on shape space (Gaussian landmarks) and distances are distance. The uniform null rejects for any concentrated sample, clustered or not, so it says nothing about clusters.

The p-value does not assume \(H = 0.5\). For each of B draws a full data set of \(n\) objects is simulated from the null (for the tangent null, the Gaussian fitted to the data; for the uniform null, \(n\) uniform shapes), \(H\) is computed on it by the same procedure, and \(p = (1 + \#\{H_b \ge H\}) / (B + 1)\).

The exponent usually recommended is the dimension of the space. With a Monte Carlo reference the choice affects power, not validity.

See also

shape_distance, shape_mean

Examples

sim <- sim_shapes3d(n = 30, sigma = 1, k = 8, seed = 1)
hopkins_shape(sim$X, B = 19, seed = 2)
#> Hopkins test of clustering tendency (tangent null)
#> H = 0.6938, p = 0.05  (m = 6, power = 1, B = 19)
